title: Utilization is time-weighted over a one-day interval so the rate cannot be gamed by momentary borrowing
content:
A.4.4.1.3.2.1.4 defines `Utilization` as "the percent of funds in the stUSDS contract that are used to fund borrowing against staked SKY," and A.4.4.1.3.2.1.4.1 constrains how it is read: "calculated as a time-weighted utilization over a one (1) day interval."

An instantaneous utilization reading would be directly manipulable, because utilization is a ratio of two user-controlled quantities. A borrower could spike it to raise a rate, or a large depositor could dilute it to suppress one, holding the position only long enough to be observed. Since the value feeds a rate that determines real payments, that is a profitable attack, not a theoretical one.

Time-weighting removes the leverage. A spike held for a minute contributes a minute's worth of weight out of a day, so manipulation costs scale with duration — an attacker must fund the distorted position for a meaningful fraction of the window to move the number, which usually costs more than the rate distortion is worth.

The one-day window is a deliberate midpoint. Shorter windows track genuine conditions faster but are cheaper to manipulate; much longer windows leave the rate stale during real liquidity crunches, exactly when it needs to be recruiting deposits. A day is long enough to make manipulation expensive and short enough that the incentive to supply responds within a business cycle.

The secondary benefit is fairness: lenders are compensated for capital that was actually deployed across the interval, rather than for whatever the ratio happened to be at a settlement instant.
description: Using a duration-weighted average instead of an instantaneous reading means a flash spike in borrowing barely moves the rate, and lenders are paid for capital actually deployed over time.
